subject: Chemistry
title: Indigo: The King of Blue Dyes
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Indigo: The King of Blue Dyes.

hook.text: Indigo has dyed clothes blue for 6,000 years. Ancient Egyptians wrapped mummies in indigo-dyed linen.

buildup.text: The Indigofera plant contains indican. Fermenting leaves converts it to indigo white, which oxidizes to deep blue.

discovery.text: Indigo bonds weakly to fibers. That's why jeans fade—the dye sits on the surface and wears off gradually.

twist.text: In 1897, BASF synthesized indigo and collapsed India's indigo farming industry. Chemistry destroyed a colonial economy.

climax.text: Today, 80,000 tons of synthetic indigo are made yearly—almost all for blue jeans. One molecule dresses the world.

punchline.text: A plant pigment that fades on purpose. That worn-in look is chemistry.

quiz.question: Why do blue jeans fade over time?
options: Indigo bonds weakly to cotton fibers and wears off the surface gradually
Sunlight breaks down the indigo molecule permanently
Washing detergent dissolves the indigo completely

details.summary: Indigo is a vat dye whose deep blue color comes from its cross-conjugated system with two carbonyl groups. The dyeing process requires chemical reduction to make it soluble, followed by reoxidation on fabric fibers. It has been used for over 6,000 years and colors every pair of blue jeans.
details.whyItMatters: Indigo's unique dyeing chemistry creates the characteristic fading pattern of denim. Synthetic indigo production was a landmark achievement in industrial chemistry that transformed the global dye industry.
takeaways: Indigo's blue comes from cross-conjugated carbonyl chromophore groups
It must be chemically reduced to dissolve, then reoxidized on fabric
Synthetic indigo replaced plant-derived indigo in the late 1800s

faq.question: Why do blue jeans fade in a way that other dyed fabrics do not?
faq.answer: Indigo molecules sit on the surface of cotton fibers rather than penetrating deeply into them. Physical abrasion at stress points like knees and pockets removes surface indigo, revealing white undyed cotton beneath. This surface-level bonding creates denim's unique wear patterns.

faq.question: How did synthetic indigo change the global economy?
faq.answer: Before synthesis, indigo was extracted from plants grown on vast plantations in India and the Americas. Adolf von Baeyer's 1880 synthesis and BASF's industrial process by 1897 made natural indigo farming unprofitable.
